scenarios.title: The Teammate's Celebration
scenarios.text: The locker room has a social life: a card game in the back, a weekly dinner, a group that goes out after home games. Everyone's waiting to see how far into it the new kicker wants to go.

choices.label: Join in, within reason
choices.result: The card game and the weekly dinner, yes; the late nights, no. By midseason you're part of the room, and nobody minds that you leave at ten.

choices.label: Pick one thing
choices.result: Just the weekly dinner. You know a few teammates well instead of all of them a little, and two of them become real friends.

choices.label: Keep to your routine
choices.result: Your routine, and nothing else: film, sleep, practice. Your kicking is sharp, and by October nobody in the room thinks to invite you anywhere.

scenarios.title: The Position Meeting
scenarios.text: Your place on the depth chart came up in a meeting you weren't invited to. The long snapper tells you about it at lunch, quietly, then goes back to his sandwich.

choices.label: Ask where you stand
choices.result: {coach} gives you an honest answer in the hallway: safe, for now, if the next month looks like the last one. It's not comfortable, and it's clear.

choices.label: Kick and say nothing
choices.result: Silence, and the best week of practice you've had since camp. Nobody calls another meeting about you, and the snapper starts eating lunch at your table.

choices.label: Call your agent
choices.result: Your agent calls the general manager, who calls {coach}. By Wednesday everyone in the building knows you asked, and {coach} is cooler with you for a while.

scenarios.title: The New Playbook
scenarios.text: A new coaching staff arrives with a new playbook and new expectations for the specialists: three hundred pages, eleven new formations, and a written test on Friday.

choices.label: Learn it cold
choices.result: Every page, cold, including the parts that aren't yours. The new coordinator notices you correcting a linebacker in the walkthrough and remembers your name.

choices.label: Learn your part
choices.result: Your part, perfectly, and nothing else. It's enough for the test, and you get a full night's sleep before it.

choices.label: Study with the unit
choices.result: A study session with the snapper and {holder} turns into a unit dinner, then a weekly tradition. Everyone passes, and you all argue about formations over dessert.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Comparison
scenarios.text: Every week, the local media compare you with another young kicker by name, in charts and columns and one very loud radio segment. You've never met him.

choices.label: Call the other kicker
choices.result: A phone call, and you're both laughing within a minute. You agree not to read anything with both your names in it, and to have dinner when your teams play.

choices.label: Put the charts on your locker
choices.result: The comparison goes up on your locker, and every practice becomes a contest. You're sharper by November, and a little more tired.

choices.label: Stop reading it
choices.result: No columns, no charts, no radio. It takes real discipline for two weeks, then it's just quiet, and you stop wondering how the other kicker is doing.

scenarios.title: The Charity Donation
scenarios.text: Your aunt calls from home: the church you grew up in needs a new roof, and she's sure you'll want to help. She has already told the whole congregation you're thinking about it.

choices.label: Give generously
choices.result: More than she asked. The church puts your name on a brass plaque by the door, which you'll be embarrassed by forever, and {parent} visits it every Sunday.

choices.label: Give what you planned
choices.result: The amount in your budget, with an explanation. She's a little disappointed and grateful anyway, and the roof gets fixed by spring.

choices.label: Run a fundraiser at home
choices.result: A fundraiser in your hometown, run with {sibling}, raises twice the money with your time instead of your account. The whole town shows up.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Advice
scenarios.text: A veteran tells you, very calmly, at lunch, how fast a career can end: his roommate from his rookie year lasted one season and now sells insurance two towns over.

choices.label: Ask what he did differently
choices.result: What did he do differently? His answer has nothing to do with kicking: he saved, he slept, he showed up early, and he never thought he was safe.

choices.label: Let it scare you
choices.result: It scares you, properly. You start saving half of every check and sleeping nine hours a night, and you check the transaction wire more than you should.

choices.label: Shrug it off
choices.result: It won't happen to you, you say with a shrug. The veteran nods slowly, like he's heard exactly that before, and finishes his lunch.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Warning
scenarios.text: Your agent warns you to be careful about where you're seen: a teammate's photo outside a nightclub at two in the morning just cost him a sponsor and a fine.

choices.label: Change your routine
choices.result: No more nights out after home games. You're bored some Saturdays and safe all of them, and the club's media staff stops looking nervous when you walk in.

choices.label: Get the real list
choices.result: A specific list of what's actually off-limits, from your agent, by text. It's shorter than you feared, and much clearer than 'be careful'.

choices.label: Brush off the warning
choices.result: You're not doing anything wrong, you insist, and keep your routine. Your agent sighs and sends a second email with the word 'please' in the subject line.

scenarios.title: The Apartment Neighbor
scenarios.text: Your neighbor works nights and practices drums at noon, which is the only hour of the day you have for a nap. It's been two weeks, and he's getting better, which is worse.

choices.label: Knock and explain
choices.result: A knock, a short explanation, and it turns out he's a fan. He moves practice to the evening and leaves two tickets to his band's show on your mat.

choices.label: Call the building manager
choices.result: The building manager makes the drumming stop within a day. So does the neighbor's friendly wave in the hallway, permanently.

choices.label: Buy good earplugs
choices.result: Very good earplugs, and you nap anyway. It works, mostly, and the neighbor waves at you every morning, never knowing.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Criticism
scenarios.text: Somebody posts a week of your bad practice clips online, set to sad music, and fans tear into you in the replies. {parent} has found it, and has been replying to strangers.

choices.label: Log off
choices.result: The apps are deleted for a week. It's quiet and it helps, and you call {parent} to ask him, gently, to stop arguing with strangers on your behalf.

choices.label: Reply with humor
choices.result: A joke about your own form, in reply, with a slow-motion clip of your worst miss. It's the most-liked reply of the week, and the tone changes.

choices.label: Save the worst one
choices.result: A screenshot of the worst reply goes on your locker. Every rep that week has a little extra in it, and the clips stop coming.

scenarios.title: The Second Contract Conversation
scenarios.text: Your agent starts talking, over a long lunch, about what your second contract could look like if you last that long. There's a napkin with numbers on it.

choices.label: Ask what lasting looks like
choices.result: What does the club actually look for in a second contract? The list is specific, and you can work on every item, starting tomorrow.

choices.label: Dream a little
choices.result: The house, the car, the security: you let yourself picture all of it. It's motivating, mostly, and you keep the napkin.

choices.label: Change the subject
choices.result: Not past this season, you say, and push the napkin back. Your agent grins and says that's exactly the right answer.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Rules
scenarios.text: The veterans post the locker room's unwritten rules on a whiteboard, and one of them is about you, in red marker: 'Kickers don't talk in team meetings.'

choices.label: Laugh and follow it
choices.result: Laughing, you follow it all season. The veterans are a little disappointed you didn't fight it; they'd already planned their responses.

choices.label: Break the rule once
choices.result: Once, in a meeting, about something that matters. The room is silent, then a captain nods, and the rule is quietly erased the next morning.

choices.label: Erase it
choices.result: Erased, during lunch. It's back the next morning in bigger letters, with a drawing of you, and the whole team signs it.

scenarios.title: The Playbook Test
scenarios.text: The special teams coordinator quizzes the rookies on the playbook, out loud, at seven in the morning, in front of the veterans. He starts with you.

choices.label: Know it cold
choices.result: Every question, answered cleanly. The coordinator moves on quickly to the next rookie, which is the highest compliment he gives.

choices.label: Bluff through it
choices.result: Two answers bluffed with confidence. The coordinator knows, and assigns you a page of the playbook to copy by hand, in pen, by Monday.

choices.label: Admit you don't know
choices.result: One answer you don't know, and you admit it and ask for the right one. The coordinator respects it, and the veterans notice.

scenarios.title: Learning the Snap Count
scenarios.text: The long snapper's rhythm is completely different from anything you had in college: faster, flatter, with a pause you can't predict. Practice is tomorrow, and the snapper doesn't do small talk.

choices.label: Ask for extra snaps
choices.result: Fifty extra snaps after practice, and he agrees with a grunt. By the end, you can hear the rhythm in your sleep, and he nods once on the way out.

choices.label: Adjust your timing alone
choices.result: Counting in your head all evening, you rebuild your approach alone in the living room. It works by the second day, mostly.

choices.label: Ask the snapper to adjust
choices.result: Can he speed up for you? He laughs and says no. Then, the next morning, without a word, he does it anyway.
